name: Big Gertie

inspiration.oldScript: Leatherface's apron, wigs and makeup were played as grotesque gender nonconformity: a big body in the wrong costume as the horror.
inspiration.newLens: A big working woman nobody looks at. Her mask is the hairnet, her horror is thirty years of invisible labor, and her Best ending is being seen, thanked and paid.

logline: Thirty years behind the steam table and not one kid ever learned her name. Now the lunch line runs all night, the mystery meat crawls out of the drains, and her hairnet hides a cleaver.
backstory: Ruthanne Bixby drove rivets into destroyer hulls at the Mare Island Navy Yard when she was eighteen. In September 1956 she took a job on the lunch line at Glimmer Falls High, and she has served there every school day since: more than two million lunches, every tray handed over with the same four words. Tray. Fork. Napkin. Next. She is six foot one, and some smart-mouthed freshman in 1957 named her Big Gertie. The name got passed down like a dare for thirty years. In 1971 a senior leaned over the sneeze guard and asked, "Do you even have a real name, Gertie?" She told him, and he laughed so hard he dropped his tray. She has not said her name in that building since, and she decided that if they would not learn hers, she would not learn theirs. This October the Heartstone woke up. Every night now Ruthanne falls asleep in her recliner above the Suds-O-Mat, and every morning she wakes with gravy on her shoes. In between, something eight feet tall in a hairnet and a stained apron walks the halls of Glimmer Falls High with a ladle like a mace and a cleaver tucked under the net. The mystery meat walks with her.

centralIssue.title: Treated like furniture
centralIssue.summary: For thirty years Ruthanne fed every kid in Glimmer Falls and nobody bothered to learn her name. Big Gertie is what happens when a person is used like a fixture until she starts to believe she is one. Learn who she is, and get the town to say thank you out loud.

poster: A towering lunch lady in a stained white apron and a hairnet stretched over the shape of a cleaver, a huge steel ladle raised over a shadowy school cafeteria, quivering gray-brown mystery meat oozing across the floor toward fleeing teens with lunch trays
portrait: Close portrait of a tall, broad-shouldered woman in her sixties with steel-gray hair under a tight hairnet, the silhouette of a cleaver pressing through the net, tired eyes that have seen everything, steam from a serving tray lighting her face from below
endingPhoto: A towering lunch lady in a stained white apron and stretched hairnet hoisting a steaming steel pot of quivering gray mystery meat over her head in a dark school kitchen, a meat cleaver on her belt, trays of sloppy food sliding off the counter, teens in letterman jackets skidding on spilled pudding as they flee through the swinging doors behind her
taunts: I've seen your face five thousand times. You've never once seen mine.
You want seconds? Nobody ever wants seconds.

clues.title: Thirty years, no name
clues.hint: The yearbook office keeps every Glimmer Light annual since 1956. Check the staff pages.

encounter.title: Cafeteria Staff (Unidentified)
encounter.place: The yearbook office, Glimmer Falls High
encounter.text: The yearbook office smells like rubber cement and deadline panic. A long shelf holds every Glimmer Light annual since 1956, the spines faded from maroon to pink. Chip Merriweather is at the light table pretending he isn't hiding in here. Someone has left a lunch tray of tater tots beside the books. They're still steaming. Nobody in the room brought them.
encounter.art: A cramped high school yearbook office, a long shelf of thirty faded maroon and pink school annuals, a preppy 17-year-old boy with side-parted chestnut hair, a pink oxford shirt and a navy blazer bent over a glowing light table, a cafeteria lunch tray of steaming tater tots sitting on the shelf beside the books, a teenager pulling one annual down, white light-table glow from below and a dim desk lamp, medium shot

choices.label: Flip to the staff page in every yearbook

success.text: 1956 through 1986: the same tall woman, the same hairnet, the same ladle, thirty times. The caption under every photo reads Cafeteria Staff. In 1971 someone typed Big Gertie (?). In 1979, unidentified. Not once her name. In the margin of this year's proof, in red ballpoint, in handwriting nobody in this office claims, someone has written: I FED YOU.
success.art: A row of open yearbooks spread across a table, each showing the same tall lunch lady in a hairnet over decades of changing fashions, the newest page scrawled with red ink in the margin

failure.text: The pages flip on their own to the cafeteria photo, year after year, and in each one the woman with the ladle is a little closer to the camera. In 1986 she's gone from the frame entirely. So are the tater tots.
failure.art: Yearbook pages flipping by themselves, a lunch lady growing closer to the camera in each photo, an empty frame on the final page and an empty tray beside it

choices.label: Ask Chip to pull the staff records for a caption

success.text: Chip digs a payroll photocopy out of the files the yearbook uses for staff names. R. BIXBY, FOOD SERVICE, HIRED SEPT 1956. He goes very quiet. "We just never asked," he says. He takes out his best class-president pen and writes RUTHANNE BIXBY on a sticky note, then presses it onto this year's proof like a promise.
success.art: A preppy teen in a sweater vest pressing a handwritten sticky note onto a yearbook proof photo of a lunch lady, an old payroll sheet beside it, his expression ashamed and determined

failure.text: Chip has a proof due at four and three student-council crises and says staff photos aren't his department. On the bulletin board behind him, every caption on every photo has changed to unidentified. Including the one of you.
failure.art: A cork bulletin board of school photos with every caption reading unidentified, a stressed teen in a sweater vest buried in paperwork in front of it

clues.title: Miss Ruthie's roasting pans
clues.hint: Every Thanksgiving the Glitter Box hosts a dinner for kids with nowhere else to go. Ask who does the cooking.

encounter.title: The Kitchen Behind the Stage
encounter.place: Backstage kitchen, The Glitter Box Playhouse
encounter.text: Behind the stage, under a rack of sequined gowns, is a kitchen nobody talks about: six enormous dented roasting pans, a wall of cast iron and a hand-lettered banner from last November that says THANK YOU MISS RUTHIE! 47 KIDS FED! Glory is ironing a feather boa. Frankie is on her headset. Neither has noticed the pot of gravy simmering on a burner nobody lit.
encounter.art: A cluttered kitchen hidden behind a backstage rack of sequined gowns, six huge dented roasting pans stacked high, a wall of cast iron skillets, a painted paper streamer from last November taped over the door, a pot of brown gravy bubbling on a cold burner, in the background a tall drag queen with a platinum bouffant wig ironing a pink feather boa, a teenager reaching for a battered recipe tin, warm stage-bulb light, medium wide shot

choices.label: Ask Glory who Miss Ruthie is

success.text: Glory sets the iron down. "Ruthanne. Every Thanksgiving since 1972, she has cooked for our kids, the ones whose families put them out for being who they are. Never stays to eat. Never lets me thank her in front of anybody." She shows you a photo: a tall woman in a hairnet surrounded by teenagers in glitter and borrowed gowns, almost smiling.
success.art: A snapshot of a tall lunch lady in a hairnet standing at a long table of laughing teens in glitter and thrift-store gowns, roasting pans and a carved turkey in front of her

failure.text: Glory is in a full rehearsal panic and shoos you out with a boa. On your way past the stove, the gravy rolls a slow, thick bubble that pops into a single word: NEXT.
failure.art: A pot of brown gravy on a stove with a bubble bursting into the shape of a word, a teenager backing away past racks of sequined costumes

choices.label: Open the battered recipe tin on the shelf

success.text: Index cards in a careful hand: Turkey for 50. Cornbread, Mare Island Style. Gravy That Forgives Everything. Each one signed R.B. Tucked in the back is a 1944 photo of a young woman in coveralls and a bandana with a rivet gun on her shoulder, and a pay stub from the Mare Island Navy Yard. Ruthanne Bixby built warships before she fed this town.
success.art: An open tin recipe box spilling handwritten index cards, a black-and-white 1940s photograph of a tall young woman in coveralls holding a rivet gun, a yellowed shipyard pay stub

failure.text: The tin snaps shut on your fingers like a mousetrap and the cards burst out across the floor. Every one of them says the same thing: TRAY. FORK. NAPKIN. NEXT. Frankie catches you and makes you scrub roasting pans until midnight.
failure.art: A teenager scrubbing an enormous roasting pan at a theatre sink late at night, a stage manager in a headset watching with arms crossed, identical index cards scattered on the floor

clues.title: The Friday Night Lady
clues.hint: For fifteen years a caller to KGLM's overnight show has dedicated a song to the kids at Glimmer Falls High every Friday. Mix keeps the logs.

encounter.title: The Request Line
encounter.text: At two in the morning the KGLM booth glows like a fish tank: reels turning, the ON AIR light burning red. Mix Bell slides a battered request log across the console. Every Friday since 1971 there's the same entry: Friday Night Lady. "Stand By Me." For the kids at the high school. Tell them to eat their vegetables. The request line starts blinking.
encounter.art: A late-night radio booth at two in the morning, reel-to-reel tapes turning, green VU meter needles glowing, a red on-air bulb lit over the door, a 17-year-old Black DJ with a high-top fade, big padded headphones and a purple satin station jacket sliding a worn spiral logbook across the console to a teenager, a beige request-line phone blinking red in the foreground, dim green and red light, medium shot over the console

choices.label: Pick up the request line yourself

success.text: A woman's voice, low and tired: "Is Marcus on? I've got my dedication." You ask her name. A long pause. "Nobody's asked me that in fifteen years. It's Ruthanne." She tells you about the boy who laughed in 1971. "Figured if they didn't want mine, I wouldn't learn theirs. Easier that way. You can't miss a face you never put a name to."
success.art: A teenager holding a curly-corded studio phone to their ear in a dim radio booth, eyes wide and gentle, the red on-air light glowing behind them

failure.text: Heavy breathing, and then a voice like a steam table: "Keep the line moving." A wet chop, like a cleaver into a cutting board, and then dial tone. The booth smells like creamed corn for a week.
failure.art: A radio booth phone dangling off its hook, a teenager recoiling, faint steam curling out of the receiver

choices.label: Ask Mix to play back his old tapes of her calls

success.text: Mix threads up a reel of old airchecks. Fifteen years of the same voice getting a little more tired every year. On the oldest tape, from spring 1971, she sounds young and bright and says her name like it's nothing: "This is Ruthanne, I work the lunch line, and I just love these kids." By 1972, she's only the Friday Night Lady.
success.art: A teen DJ in headphones threading an old reel-to-reel tape, a label marked 1971 on the box, a teenager listening intently beside the glowing console

failure.text: The reel plays backward with a hiss like a steam table, and every needle on the board pins into the red. Mix has to kill the transmitter, and four thousand insomniacs in Glimmer Falls hear thirty seconds of dead air and the clatter of trays.
failure.art: A radio console with every meter pinned in the red, a teen DJ slamming a kill switch, a reel of tape spinning backward in a blur

signature.title: The Line
signature.text: You don't remember coming to school. You're holding a beige tray in a cafeteria lit by one buzzing tube, standing in a line that stretches back into the dark: every kid in Glimmer Falls since 1956, in letterman jackets and poodle skirts and Members Mostly jackets, shuffling forward without a word. At the steam table, a tall shape in a hairnet ladles something that moves. "Tray," it says. "Fork. Napkin. Next."
signature.art: A school cafeteria at midnight lit by one flickering fluorescent tube, a long line of pale silent teenagers stretching back into darkness, letterman jackets, poodle skirts and nylon windbreakers from three decades, each holding a beige tray, a teenager in pajamas standing in the line holding a tray, at the steam table a towering broad-shouldered woman in her sixties in a tight hairnet and stained white apron ladling gray food that wriggles, cold green-white light, wide shot along the line

choices.label: Look her in the eye and say thank you

success.text: The ladle stops halfway. The whole line goes silent. For one second you see under the hairnet: a tired woman's face, astonished. "Well," she says, "nobody's ever..." The cafeteria fades into morning, and on your tray sits a perfect cinnamon roll, still warm.
success.art: A towering lunch lady frozen mid-scoop, her stern face softening in astonishment, a teenager holding a tray with a single glowing cinnamon roll, the dark cafeteria dissolving into morning light

failure.text: She doesn't hear you over the clatter of thirty years of trays. A scoop of Salisbury Surprise slaps onto your tray and starts crawling up your arm. You wake in bed with gravy in your sneakers.
failure.art: A lump of gray-brown mystery meat crawling up a teenager's sleeve from a lunch tray, a hairnetted giant already turning to the next kid in line

choices.label: Duck under the rail and bolt for the kitchen door

success.text: You slide under the sneeze guard, past the dish pit, past a walk-in freezer humming like a hornet's nest, and out the loading dock into the cold. You wake in your own bed, panting, clutching a carton of chocolate milk you definitely did not pay for.
success.art: A teenager sliding under a cafeteria sneeze guard and sprinting through a steamy school kitchen toward a loading dock door glowing with moonlight

failure.text: "NO CUTTING." The cleaver comes down on the tray rail an inch from your fingers, and the line closes around you like water. When you look up you're at the very back again, behind 1962.
failure.art: A cleaver embedded in a steel tray rail inches from a teenager's hand, the ghostly lunch line closing around them

choices.label: Eat whatever she serves without a single complaint

success.text: It tastes like Sunday dinner at somebody's grandma's house. The mystery meat on your tray stops wriggling and settles with something like a purr. Behind the steam table, the giant grunts. It might be approval. It might be the first compliment she's had since Nixon.
success.art: A teenager bravely eating from a lunch tray, eyes closed in surprised delight, the mystery meat on the tray resting contentedly, a towering lunch lady watching with a grunt

failure.text: It eats back. You spend the rest of the dream wrestling your lunch across the cafeteria floor while the line shuffles past without looking down.
failure.art: A teenager wrestling a writhing blob of mystery meat on a cafeteria floor while a line of ghostly students steps around them

signature.title: The Mystery Meat Is Moving
signature.text: Barnaby howls at midnight. Then you hear it: a wet, cheerful squelch from every storm drain on Crystal Street. Gray-brown blobs of Salisbury Surprise ooze up out of the gutters, roll across the lawns and gather into one quivering mound the size of a station wagon, with two canned peas for eyes. It smells exactly like Tuesday. It wants to form a line.
signature.art: A suburban street at one in the morning, gray-brown lumps of meat loaf oozing up out of every storm drain, rolling across the lawns and merging in the road into one quivering brown mound the size of a station wagon with two round green peas for eyes, a tricolor basset hound with long ears and a red bandana howling on a porch, teenagers in pajamas with a can of hairspray and a whistle at the curb, orange streetlight, wide shot

choices.label: Blast it with Aqua-Glow until it hardens

success.text: A choking cloud of Max Hold, and the meat lacquers into a shiny brown sculpture right in the middle of the Okafors' lawn. It will stay there until Thanksgiving. Mrs. Okafor puts a pumpkin on it and calls it art.
success.art: A glossy hardened blob of brown mystery meat shaped like a lumpy statue on a suburban lawn, a teenager lowering a can of hairspray in a cloud of mist

failure.text: It drinks the hairspray. It gets glossier. It gets bigger. Then it sneezes, and you are launched backward into the Okafors' hedge with your hair standing straight up and locked that way for two days.
failure.art: A teenager flying backward into a hedge with their hair blasted straight up, a giant glossy blob of mystery meat mid-sneeze in the street

choices.label: Blow a whistle and march it single file

success.text: One sharp blast and the meat obeys like every freshman ever born: it splits into a dozen blobs, forms a single-file line and squelches off down Crystal Street toward the high school, where it files neatly into the dumpster and lies down.
success.art: A line of small mystery meat blobs marching single file down a moonlit suburban street toward a school dumpster, a figure with a coach's whistle leading them

failure.text: It obeys too well. It lines up behind you, and only you, and follows you all night, squelching at your heels. In the morning your mother asks why the porch smells like gravy.
failure.art: A long line of mystery meat blobs following a dismayed teenager up their porch steps at dawn, the front door opening on a confused parent

signature.title: Family Dinner
signature.place: The Home Ec classroom, Glimmer Falls High, 2 a.m.
signature.text: You wake up seated at a long dinner table in the Home Ec room, a paper napkin tucked into your collar. Around you sit the classroom's dress-form mannequins, each wearing a hairnet and an apron, each with a lunch tray set neatly in front of it. A 1958 filmstrip called Feeding the Family clicks on the wall projector. Big Gertie ducks through the supply closet door carrying a casserole the size of a bathtub, sets it down at the head of the table, and waits. Nobody has ever stayed for dinner before.
signature.art: A school home economics classroom at two in the morning, a long dinner table with a white tablecloth, dress-form mannequins seated in every chair wearing hairnets and aprons with lunch trays in front of them, a teenager sitting at the table with a paper napkin tucked into their collar, a filmstrip projector throwing a pale square of light on the wall, a towering woman in a hairnet and white apron ducking through a closet doorway carrying a steaming casserole dish the size of a bathtub, warm projector glow and dark corners, wide shot

choices.label: Take a big bite and compliment the cook by name

success.text: "This is really good," you say, and you mean it: tuna, egg noodles, crushed potato chips, somebody's mother's recipe. Big Gertie sits down for the first time in thirty years. The mannequins tip their hairnets to her, one by one. When you wake up, there is a recipe card in your pocket in neat block print, signed R.B.
success.art: A towering lunch lady seated at the head of a dinner table for the first time, her shoulders relaxed, a teenager smiling with a forkful of casserole, mannequins in hairnets tipping their heads toward her

failure.text: Your mouth is full and the compliment comes out as a muffled honk. She takes it for a complaint. The filmstrip speeds up, the mannequins swivel to stare, and the casserole slowly slides itself down the table toward you, wanting to be finished.
failure.art: A giant casserole dish sliding down a long dinner table toward a teenager with puffed cheeks, dress-form mannequins in hairnets all turned toward them, a filmstrip flickering on the wall

choices.label: Slip under the tablecloth and crawl for the door

success.text: Under the tablecloth it is dark and smells like starch. You crawl past a forest of mannequin legs and the hem of a huge stained apron, and out into the hall. Behind you, a long, tired sigh. She is clearing your place setting, carefully, like she always does.
success.art: A teenager crawling beneath a long tablecloth past mannequin legs and the hem of a stained apron, a strip of hallway light glowing at the far end

failure.text: The tablecloth goes up like a curtain. Big Gertie is crouched at the far end, eye level with you, ladle in hand. "Elbows off the floor," she says, and you spend the rest of the dream sitting up very straight, eating everything on your tray, one pea at a time.
failure.art: A towering lunch lady crouched at the end of a dinner table lifting the tablecloth to reveal a startled teenager on hands and knees, ladle raised

choices.label: Roll up your sleeves and do the dishes beside her

success.text: You scrub. She dries. Neither of you says anything for a long while, and it is the most comfortable silence of your life. Halfway through the stack she starts humming a Patsy Cline song, very low, and then she hands you the last dry plate like it is a medal.
success.art: A teenager with rolled sleeves scrubbing dishes at a deep steel sink beside a towering lunch lady drying a plate, steam rising, the two working side by side in warm lamplight

failure.text: The stack never ends. For every plate you wash, two more slide out of the pass-through window, crusted with thirty years of gravy. By dawn your fingers are pruned to raisins and the pile still reaches the ceiling tiles.
failure.art: A teenager at a steel sink buried behind a towering stack of dirty plates reaching the ceiling, more plates sliding out of a pass-through window

signature.title: The Car Won't Start
signature.place: The faculty parking lot, Glimmer Falls High, 11 p.m.
signature.text: The '71 Roadhawk Joey borrowed off Rusty's lot has never failed him, and tonight it coughs, clicks and dies in the faculty lot. Through the fogged rear window you see the cafeteria loading dock slide open. A tall shape in a hairnet steps into the floodlight, and the night fills with a sound you know from every school day of your life: the high, grinding whine of the industrial potato masher, revving. It starts walking toward the car. It is in no hurry at all.
signature.art: A rusty 1971 muscle car stalled in a dark high school parking lot at eleven at night, two teenagers peering out through a fogged rear window, a lean Diné teenager with a low ponytail and an orange work shirt in the driver's seat, beyond them a cafeteria loading dock door sliding open in a hard white floodlight and a towering woman in a hairnet and white apron stepping out holding a huge industrial potato masher, fog in the floodlight, wide shot from behind the car

choices.label: Pop the steering column and hotwire it

success.text: Two wires, one spark, and the Roadhawk roars. You peel out of the lot as the potato masher bites into the space where your bumper was. In the rearview mirror she stands alone under the floodlight, watching you go, and for one strange second she lifts a hand like she is waving goodbye to a bus.
success.art: A muscle car roaring out of a school parking lot with its taillights blazing, a lone lunch lady standing under a floodlight behind it lifting one hand in a wave

failure.text: The wires spark, the dome light dies, and the horn sticks on, blaring across the whole lot. The masher stops whining. In the sudden quiet a shadow falls across the windshield, and a ladle taps the glass three times, politely. Tray. Fork. Napkin.
failure.art: A huge shadow falling across a car windshield at night, a soup ladle tapping on the glass, teenagers inside clutching sparking wires under the dashboard

choices.label: Jump out and push-start it down the hill

success.text: You throw your shoulder into the trunk and shove. The Roadhawk rolls, gathers speed down the bus lane, coughs and catches. You dive into the back seat through the open door like a stunt double. Behind you, the potato masher winds down with a disappointed groan.
success.art: A teenager diving into the open back door of a rolling car speeding down a school bus lane, exhaust smoke curling, a hairnetted giant far behind in the floodlight

failure.text: The car rolls three feet and settles into a pothole with a clunk. You look up from the bumper straight into a stained apron. "Pushing in line," says Big Gertie. "Back of the line." You wake up at the very end of the carpool queue, in your pajamas, at dawn.
failure.art: A teenager bent behind a stalled car bumper looking up at a towering lunch lady in a stained apron looming over them in the floodlight

choices.label: Roll down the window and offer her a ride home

success.text: "You need a lift, ma'am? It's late." The masher clicks off. She folds herself into the back seat with her knees around her ears, hairnet brushing the roof, and the Roadhawk starts on the first try. You drop her outside the Suds-O-Mat. "Thirty years," she mutters, climbing out, "and I always took the bus."
success.art: A towering lunch lady folded into the back seat of a small muscle car with her knees up, hairnet brushing the roof, teenagers in front glancing back nervously, a glowing laundromat sign outside

failure.text: She bends to the window and studies you for a long moment, like a face she has seen five thousand times. "You don't know where I live," she says. "Nobody does." The masher revs, and the tires go flat one by one, gently, like sighs.
failure.art: A towering lunch lady bending to peer into a car window at night, her face shadowed under a hairnet, the car tires sagging flat in the floodlight

signature.title: I'll Be Right Back
signature.place: The Fall Lock-In, Glimmer Falls High gym, 1 a.m.
signature.text: The student council's overnight Fall Lock-In is winding down: sleeping bags on the gym floor, a dead boombox, a mountain of pizza crusts. Chip Merriweather stands up and stretches. "I'm getting pudding cups from the cafeteria," he says. "I'll be right back." That was twenty minutes ago. Now, from far down the dark hallway, comes a sound like a ladle being dragged along every locker, one at a time, getting closer.
signature.art: A high school gymnasium at one in the morning scattered with sleeping bags, pizza boxes and a dead boombox, four teenagers sitting up in their sleeping bags staring toward the open double doors, beyond the doors a long dark hallway of lockers with a dim yellow glow at its far end and a long shadow stretching across the floor, blue moonlight through high gym windows, wide shot from the floor

choices.label: Grab a flashlight and go after Chip

success.text: Your beam finds Chip in the cafeteria doorway, frozen, holding a pudding cup. Big Gertie looms over him with her ladle raised, and then she sees your light, sees that somebody came looking. She lowers the ladle, takes a spoon from her apron and puts it in Chip's hand. "You forgot a spoon," she says, and walks into the dark.
success.art: A flashlight beam cutting across a dark cafeteria doorway onto a frozen preppy teenager holding a pudding cup, a towering lunch lady lowering her ladle and offering him a spoon

failure.text: The flashlight dies halfway down the hall. In the dark, the ladle scrapes the locker right beside your head, and a voice says, "Hall pass?" You run back to the gym. Chip turns up at dawn in a hairnet, wiping tables, with no memory of the night.
failure.art: A teenager running down a pitch-dark school hallway clutching a dead flashlight, a long steel ladle scraping along the lockers behind them, a towering hairnetted shadow at the far end of the hall

choices.label: Break into the office and call everyone back on the PA

success.text: You jimmy the office door and flip the PA to ALL ROOMS. "Chip Merriweather to the gym, please. Chip Merriweather to the gym." Down the hall a door bangs, sneakers squeak, and Chip skids in clutching an armful of pudding cups. Then the speaker crackles, and a deep voice says, "And thank the kitchen."
success.art: A teenager leaning into a school office microphone at night under a glowing desk lamp, a preppy teenager skidding into a gym doorway clutching an armful of pudding cups

failure.text: You key the PA, and the voice that comes out is not yours. "Tray," it booms through every speaker in the building. "Fork. Napkin. Next." The whole lock-in shuffles into a line in their sleeping bags, and you spend the night standing at the end of it.
failure.art: Teenagers in sleeping bags shuffling into a single file line across a dark gym, a school loudspeaker on the wall glowing, one teenager staring at a microphone in horror

choices.label: Slide a thank-you napkin under the kitchen door

success.text: You write THANK YOU FOR LUNCH on a napkin and slide it under the kitchen door. A long silence. Then the door swings open and Chip walks out holding a tray of pudding cups, one for every kid at the lock-in. "She said I was the first kid in thirty years to ask what was for dessert," he whispers.
success.art: A school kitchen door swinging open into a dark hallway, a preppy teenager stepping out carrying a tray stacked with pudding cups, warm kitchen light spilling around him

failure.text: The napkin slides back out under the door, folded into a neat triangle. Written on it in block print: SEE ME AFTER LUNCH. You do not sleep for the rest of the lock-in, and every time you close your eyes you hear a ladle tapping.
failure.art: A folded paper napkin lying on a school hallway floor in a strip of light under a kitchen door, a nervous teenager crouched beside it in the dark

signature.title: The Walk-In
signature.text: The heavy freezer door thunks shut behind you. Frost on everything. Tater-tot boxes stacked to the ceiling, and hanging from steel hooks in a neat row, rimed white, are the letterman jackets, cheer sweaters and headphone tape players of every kid who skipped her line this week. Down the aisle comes the scrape of a cleaver on a sharpening steel, slow and patient. "I know you," says Big Gertie. "I know every face. I just never bothered with the names."
signature.art: The inside of a frost-covered cafeteria walk-in freezer at three in the morning, cardboard boxes of tater tots stacked to the ceiling, letterman jackets, cheer sweaters and headphone tape players hanging in a row from steel meat hooks rimed in white frost, a shivering teenager in a jacket pressed against the shelves, at the far end of the aisle a towering woman in a hairnet and apron sharpening a cleaver on a steel, cold blue light and white breath clouds, medium wide shot down the aisle

choices.label: Tell her your name and ask for hers

success.text: You tell her your name. You ask for hers. The cleaver stops on the steel. Frost melts off a nametag on her apron you never noticed: R. BIXBY. "Ruthanne," she whispers, trying it out like a word in a foreign language. Behind you, the freezer door clicks open.
success.art: A towering lunch lady in a frosted freezer lowering her cleaver, frost melting off a small nametag on her apron, a teenager standing their ground with an open hand

failure.text: "Names," she says, "are for people who stay." The light goes out. You spend the night pounding on the inside of the door and wake up at home with frost in your eyebrows and one shoe missing.
failure.art: A teenager pounding on the inside of a dark freezer door, breath fogging, frost forming on their eyebrows

choices.label: Wedge the door with a lunch tray and drag the jackets out

success.text: The tray wedges, the door groans, and you haul out two frozen letterman jackets before it slams. In the morning, two kids who'd been home sick with mysterious chills wake up warm and starving. You find a few quarters in the pockets, and decide that's a fair reward.
success.art: A teenager squeezing out of a freezer door propped by a bent lunch tray, arms full of frost-covered letterman jackets, a cleaver flashing in the dark behind them

failure.text: The tray snaps like a cracker. The cleaver thunks into the shelf beside your ear and a box of tots explodes over your head. You get out, but you leave something behind, hanging on a hook.
failure.art: A cleaver lodged in a freezer shelf beside a teenager's head, frozen tater tots raining down, the teenager diving for a narrowing gap in the door

choices.label: Burrow into the tater-tot boxes and hold very still

success.text: She passes so close you could touch her apron. Up close you see what nobody has seen in thirty years: tears freezing on her cheeks. She doesn't find you. When she's gone, you slip out, and you can't stop thinking about her face.
success.art: A teenager hidden among frozen cardboard boxes, peering at a towering lunch lady passing by with frozen tears glittering on her cheeks

failure.text: A box tips. An avalanche of frozen tots buries you to the neck, and a huge hand plucks you out by the collar. "Hiding from lunch," she says. "In my day we were grateful."
failure.art: A huge hand lifting a teenager by the collar out of a pile of spilled frozen tater tots, a hairnetted giant scowling in the blue freezer light

signature.title: Part of the Furniture
signature.text: You wake up and you cannot move, because you are a chair: molded orange plastic, chrome legs, bolted into a row at table nine. The cafeteria is full of dream students clattering trays, and every one of them drops onto you without a glance, eats, scrapes back and leaves. Nobody says excuse me. Nobody even looks down. After the last bell, a huge shadow in a hairnet lowers herself onto you with a groan, the first time she has sat down all day, and the plastic creaks under thirty years of tired.
signature.art: A dim school cafeteria after hours, rows of molded orange plastic chairs on chrome legs bolted along long tables, one chair at the end with a startled teenager's face pressed into its plastic seat back, a towering broad-shouldered woman in her sixties with a tight hairnet and stained apron lowering herself onto that chair with a tired groan and a hand on her knee, trays stacked on the steam table behind, a single warm light over the serving line, medium shot

choices.label: Hold perfectly steady and let her rest

success.text: You lock every chrome leg and hold. She sighs, long and deep, and her chin sinks to her apron. For ten whole minutes Big Gertie sleeps, the first break she has taken since 1956, and when she wakes she pats your seat back like a good horse. You wake in bed with sore shoulders and the strange feeling that you did someone a kindness.
success.art: A towering lunch lady dozing peacefully in an orange plastic cafeteria chair, chin resting on her stained apron, the chair glowing softly, dim fluorescent light humming over a row of stacked beige trays

failure.text: Your leg buckles with a plastic crack and she lands on the linoleum with a thump that rattles every tray in the room. She looks at the broken chair for a long time. "Even the furniture," she mutters, and drags you off toward the dumpster by one leg.
failure.art: A towering lunch lady sitting stunned on a cafeteria floor beside a broken orange plastic chair, trays rattling on the long tables, her hairnet askew, one chrome chair leg snapped in her big hand

choices.label: Creak out "Excuse me!" in your loudest chair voice

success.text: "EXCUSE ME," squeaks the chair. Every dream student freezes mid-bite and stares down at their seat in horror. Then, one by one, they stand up, push their chairs in and mumble sorry. Behind the steam table, Big Gertie lets out one short bark of a laugh, the first anyone has heard from her in years.
success.art: A dream cafeteria full of startled teenagers in clothes from three decades standing up and pushing in their orange plastic chairs, a tall lunch lady behind the steam table laughing in surprise, ladle in hand

failure.text: Your voice comes out as one long, rude squeak, and the whole cafeteria laughs at the chair. Then they sit down harder. You spend the rest of the dream being tipped back on two legs by a 1974 sophomore who will not stop.
failure.art: A shaggy-haired teenager in a 1970s jacket rocking back on two legs of an orange plastic chair, a crowded dream cafeteria laughing around him, trays and milk cartons on every table

choices.label: Rock on your chrome legs until you tip over and wake up

success.text: You rock, and rock, and topple with a crash that echoes like a dropped tray. You wake up on your bedroom floor, tangled in your blanket. On your desk sits a single chrome chair leg, still faintly warm.
success.art: A teenager waking on a bedroom floor tangled in a patchwork blanket at night, a single chrome chair leg lying on the desk beside a glowing lamp, moonlight slanting through the window

failure.text: You topple into the stack of chairs by the stage and get stacked yourself, ten chairs high, at the very bottom. It takes until dawn to wriggle free. You wake up with the print of a plastic seat pressed into your cheek.
failure.art: A teetering stack of orange plastic cafeteria chairs ten high beside a school stage, a teenager's face peeking out from the bottom chair, pale dawn light at the tall windows

signature.title: The Night Shift
signature.text: The only place open in Glimmer Falls at three in the morning is Donut Dynasty, and tonight something is wrong with the waitress. Bernadette has poured coffee here for nineteen years, and right now she is going gray and see-through, like a snapshot left too long in a sunny window. The customers keep ordering from her without looking up, and every order fades her a little more, while a fresh hairnet waits on a hook by the kitchen door. It is happening all over town this week: the crossing guard, the night janitor at the bank, the bag boy at Thriftee-Mart. In the back booth, folded into a seat too small for her, Big Gertie sips black coffee and watches with tired, knowing eyes.
signature.art: A neon-lit all-night donut shop on a highway at three in the morning, a middle-aged waitress in a pink uniform pouring coffee as her body fades gray and translucent from the feet up, truckers and night-shift workers hunched over plates at the counter, a clean hairnet hanging on a hook by the kitchen door, a teenager at the counter staring at the waitress, and in the small back booth a towering woman in a hairnet sipping black coffee, pink neon and fluorescent light, wide shot

choices.label: Ask the waitress her name, and actually listen to the answer

success.text: "Bernadette," she says, surprised, and color floods back into her cheeks like someone turned up a dial. She tells you about her kids, her bad knee, the regular who tips in pennies. From the back booth comes the creak of vinyl: Big Gertie is leaning out to listen too. When you leave, there is a quarter under your saucer and a napkin printed in neat block capitals: SHE ALWAYS REMEMBERS HOW I TAKE IT.
success.art: A waitress in a pink uniform glowing back to full color behind a donut shop counter, smiling at a teenager on a stool, a tall lunch lady leaning out of a back booth to listen, neon light on the coffee pots

failure.text: She opens her mouth, and a trucker shouts "Refill!" right over her. She turns to pour, and turns grayer, and when she turns back she does not remember you asked. The hairnet on the hook sways, though there is no draft.
failure.art: A gray translucent waitress pouring coffee for a burly trucker at a neon donut counter, a teenager reaching out toward her, a hairnet swaying on a hook beside the kitchen door

choices.label: Grab a bus tub and clear every table so her shift can end

success.text: Mugs, plates, crumbs, ashtrays, sugar caddies: you move faster than you have ever moved in your life. When the last table gleams, the clock over the register jumps to six and the shift is over. Bernadette unties her apron, solid and pink-cheeked and blinking, and the hairnet slides off its hook and dissolves into steam.
success.art: A teenager racing between booths in a neon donut shop carrying a gray bus tub piled with mugs, a wall clock over the register jumping to six, a smiling waitress untying her apron in relief

failure.text: For every mug you clear, two more appear, ringed with coffee. The bell over the door keeps jingling and the orders keep coming, and by dawn you are wearing a paper hat and refilling a deputy's cup while he looks right through you.
failure.art: A teenager in a paper hat pouring coffee for a deputy at a donut counter at dawn, the deputy gazing straight through them, stacks of dirty coffee mugs multiplying on every table

choices.label: Drop a full tray of mugs so the whole room has to look up

success.text: CRASH. Every head in Donut Dynasty snaps up, and for the first time all night they see her: Bernadette, standing in the middle of the floor with a coffee pot, solid and furious. "Who's going to sweep that up?" she demands, and three customers jump to help. In the back booth, Big Gertie raises her cup to you, very slightly.
success.art: Shattered coffee mugs on a checkered donut shop floor, every customer turning to stare at a waitress standing tall with a coffee pot, a tall lunch lady in a back booth raising her cup

failure.text: Crash, and every head snaps up and stares straight at you. Not one of them looks at Bernadette. The manager hands you a broom, and you spend the rest of the night sweeping up mugs that keep breaking themselves all over again.
failure.art: A teenager sweeping shattered coffee mugs across a checkered donut shop floor under buzzing neon, customers staring at them, broken mugs magically reassembling and toppling on the counter

signature.title: The Dish Machine
signature.place: The cafeteria dish room, Glimmer Falls High, 2 a.m. the night before Halloween
signature.text: At two in the morning the dish-return belt starts up by itself, and it is carrying people. Your crew rides it in a slow line, sitting on trays, toward the dish machine: a steel tunnel the size of a boxcar, roaring with scalding spray and whirling brushes that rev like chainsaws. On the far side, in the steam, Big Gertie stacks clean trays in towers to the ceiling, every one of the two million she has handed out. "Everything comes back to the kitchen," she says, without looking up. "Everything. Nobody ever asks who washes it." Tomorrow is Halloween, and the belt is speeding up.
signature.art: A steaming school dish room at two in the morning, four teenagers riding beige plastic trays along a slow conveyor belt toward a roaring stainless-steel dish machine tunnel the size of a boxcar with whirling brushes and jets of scalding spray, a big red emergency stop button on the wall, on the far side in the steam a towering woman in a hairnet stacking clean trays in towers to the ceiling, white steam and green emergency light, wide shot

choices.label: Leap off the belt and slam the big red emergency stop

success.text: You jump, skid across wet tile and slap the red button with your whole hand. The belt shudders and stops an inch from the brushes. In the sudden quiet Big Gertie looks up through the steam, straight at you, a kid standing in her kitchen at two in the morning. "Huh," she says. "Nobody's ever stopped the line before."
success.art: A teenager slapping a big red emergency button on a steel wall of a steamy dish room, a conveyor of riders halted inches from whirling brushes, a towering lunch lady looking up through the steam

failure.text: You jump short, and the belt carries you into the tunnel with everyone else: hot spray, whirling brushes, the smell of thirty years of gravy. You come out the far end squeaky clean and stacked neatly in a tray rack. You wake up with pruned fingers and your hair parted straight down the middle.
failure.art: A dripping squeaky-clean teenager wedged sideways in a steel tray rack at the end of a dish machine tunnel, steam billowing, scrub brushes spinning behind them, hair neatly parted down the middle

choices.label: Grab a towel and race her stacking trays, cafeteria song and all

success.text: You snatch trays off the belt and wipe, stack, wipe, stack, while your crew belts out the jingle from the 1958 nutrition filmstrip. You keep up for nearly a minute, which is fifty seconds longer than you expected. Big Gertie watches you sweat, and something like a grin cracks her face. "Thirty years of this," she says. "Now you know."
success.art: A sweating teenager with a dish towel racing to stack beige trays beside a towering lunch lady in a steamy dish room, friends singing on the conveyor belt, tray towers rising to the ceiling

failure.text: A tower of trays wobbles, leans and comes down on you like an avalanche of beige plastic. Big Gertie restacks it in four seconds flat while you are still on the floor. "Amateurs," she says, almost fondly.
failure.art: An avalanche of beige plastic lunch trays tumbling onto a teenager on a wet dish room floor, a towering lunch lady calmly restacking them at blurring speed in the steam

choices.label: Flip the trays over and read what's scratched underneath

success.text: Thirty years of kids have scratched the undersides: hearts, band names, ADAM WAS HERE 1969. At the very bottom of the oldest stack, one tray is scratched in careful block print: R.B., SEPT 1956, FIRST DAY. You hold it up. Big Gertie goes very still, and the belt grinds to a stop by itself.
success.art: A teenager holding up an old scratched lunch tray in a steamy dish room, decades of carved initials and hearts on its underside, a towering lunch lady frozen mid-stack, the conveyor belt halted

failure.text: You flip one tray, and the whole stack flips back. Every tray in the room turns over at once with a deafening clatter, and the oldest one is lost in the avalanche. Somewhere under that pile, something scratched with a name is waiting, but not tonight.
failure.art: Hundreds of beige lunch trays flipping through the air at once in a steamy dish room, a teenager ducking under the clattering cascade, a towering lunch lady standing calmly in the steam

finale.title: Last Call at the Lunch Line
finale.place: Glimmer Falls High cafeteria, Halloween night
finale.text: On Halloween the whole town comes to lunch. The cafeteria has grown enormous and endless, every table full of neighbors in costume eating gray food with their heads down, nobody looking up. The steam table runs the length of the room, and behind it Big Gertie towers to the ceiling tiles, hairnet stretched over a cleaver like a shark's fin, ladle as big as a canoe paddle. "Thirty years," she booms. "Two million lunches. And not one of you ever looked up."
finale.art: An endless school cafeteria on Halloween night, long tables full of townspeople in costumes eating gray food with heads bowed, a steam table running the whole length of the room, behind it a gigantic woman in a stretched hairnet and stained white apron towering to the ceiling tiles, a cleaver tucked into her hairnet, a ladle the size of a canoe paddle in her fist, four teenagers in homemade costumes standing in the aisle facing her, green fluorescent light and orange steam, low wide shot

choices.label: Flip the steam table and pull the plug on the line

success.text: The steam table goes over with a crash like a car wreck and the steam dies in a long hiss. Big Gertie shrinks and shrinks until she is a tired woman asleep in a plastic chair by the dish pit. The town wakes up in costume, confused, and goes home. Nobody thinks to ask who she was.
success.art: A long steel steam table crashing over in a cloud of steam, a giant lunch lady shrinking into an ordinary tired woman asleep in a plastic chair, costumed townspeople blinking awake

failure.text: The steam table doesn't budge. The ladle scoops you up like a dumpling and sets you on a tray. "Next," she says, without looking at you.
failure.art: A teenager sitting stunned on a giant lunch tray, scooped by an enormous ladle, a hairnetted giant already turning away

choices.label: Start a food fight so big she can't run the line

success.text: You hurl the first tater tot. Then the whole town is flinging creamed corn and jello cubes and laughing, and nobody's head is down anymore. Nobody can run a lunch line in that kind of chaos, and the cafeteria dissolves around you in a shower of green jello.
success.art: An explosive cafeteria food fight with townspeople in Halloween costumes flinging jello, corn and tater tots, a giant lunch lady staring in dismay as the walls dissolve

failure.text: Every tot you throw she catches on a tray without looking. Then she sends them all back at once, two million of them, and you go down under a hot golden avalanche.
failure.art: A wall of tater tots flying back across a cafeteria toward a teenager, a giant lunch lady flicking a tray like a catapult

choices.label: Say her name, and get the whole room to say thank you

success.text: "Ruthanne Bixby," you say, loud. "Mare Island riveter. Thanksgiving cook. Friday Night Lady." You hold up the yearbook with Chip's sticky note. One by one, the neighbors lift their heads from their trays. "Thank you, Ruthanne." Two million thank yous, all at once. The cleaver clatters onto the steam table. The hairnet slips, and she's only a tall woman in an apron, crying and laughing, telling everybody to eat their vegetables. Then she asks you, finally, for your name.
success.art: A vast cafeteria full of costumed townspeople raising their heads and applauding, a tall lunch lady shrinking to human size with tears and laughter, her cleaver dropped, a teen holding up a yearbook with a handwritten note

failure.text: Your voice is swallowed by the clatter of trays. Nobody looks up from their plates. You know every word you need to say, but the room isn't ready to hear it yet.
failure.art: A teenager shouting into a sea of bowed heads in an endless cafeteria, trays clattering, a giant lunch lady looming, oblivious

choices.label: Pull out a chair and serve her a tray, like the first nights she finally sat down

success.text: You drag a plastic chair into the aisle, pull it out for her, and hand her a tray: "Tray. Fork. Napkin. Sit." It is the trick those first nights taught you, at the dinner table and on the lunch line: in thirty years, nobody ever served the server. Big Gertie stares at the chair, then sits, and a lunch line cannot run with its cook sitting down. The endless cafeteria folds up around her like a card table, and the town blinks awake in costume while she dozes off with a tray on her knees.
success.art: A giant lunch lady sitting down in an orange plastic chair in a cafeteria aisle with a lunch tray on her knees, a costumed teenager handing her a fork, the endless cafeteria walls folding away into the night

failure.text: She looks at the chair like it is a trap. "Sitting's for people with somewhere to be," she says, and kicks it into the dish pit. The line lurches forward again, but she glances back at the chair once, and that look is something you can work with.
failure.art: A towering lunch lady kicking an orange plastic chair across a cafeteria toward a steaming dish pit, a costumed teenager holding an untouched tray, the endless lunch line shuffling forward

choices.label: Bang a ladle on the steam table and call a walkout, for the night shift you stood up for midweek

success.text: You climb onto the steam table and bang a ladle like a gavel. "Kitchen's on strike! Nobody eats until somebody says thank you!" Out of the steam step the people her nightmare grayed out midweek, the ones the town looks right through: the donut-shop waitress, the night janitor, the crossing guard, setting down their mops and coffee pots beside you. Big Gertie looks at the picket line forming in her own cafeteria; nobody has ever stood next to her before. Her ladle comes down slowly, and the endless room shrinks back to an ordinary cafeteria full of confused neighbors in costume.
success.art: A costumed teenager standing on a long steel steam table banging a ladle, a row of tired workers in uniforms setting down mops and coffee pots beside them, a giant lunch lady lowering her ladle in astonishment

failure.text: The ladle clangs, and the clatter of two million trays swallows it whole. The gray shapes in the steam hang back, not sure yet that anyone will stand with them. Big Gertie plucks the ladle out of your hand and sets you gently back in line, but she keeps glancing toward the steam.
failure.art: A giant lunch lady plucking a ladle from a costumed teenager's hand, gray shadowy workers hovering hesitantly in clouds of cafeteria steam, rows of townspeople bent over trays

choices.label: Write her real name on a thank-you napkin, like the night before Halloween, and pass it down every table

success.text: You write THANK YOU, RUTHANNE on a paper napkin, the way the night before Halloween taught you, and pass it down the nearest table. Your neighbors look up to read it, then sign it and pass it on: the PTA president, the Channel 6 weatherman, three decades of her old students, until it comes back to you covered in names and you set it on her tray. Big Gertie reads every single one. The cleaver slides out of her hairnet and clatters onto the steam table, and she is a tall woman in an apron, laughing and crying, who looks down at you and finally asks your name.
success.art: A tall lunch lady shrinking to human size behind a steam table, tears and laughter on her face, reading a paper napkin covered in handwriting, costumed townspeople looking up from their trays and smiling

failure.text: The napkin gets halfway down the first table before someone uses it to wipe up spilled gravy. Big Gertie watches it happen. You know exactly what she needs to hear, but the room is not looking up yet.
failure.art: A crumpled paper napkin soaking in spilled gravy on a crowded cafeteria table, bowed heads over trays, a giant lunch lady watching from behind the steam table with a heavy sigh

best.title: Ruthanne Bixby Day
best.text: On November first the school board names the cafeteria the Ruthanne Bixby Dining Hall, and the whole kitchen staff finally gets the raise they've been asking for since 1979. Every staff photo in the 1987 Glimmer Light has a name under it. Ruthanne retires at Thanksgiving with a party at the Glitter Box, where two hundred former students line up to say her name to her face. She learns yours. She never forgets it, and she still yells it across the street when she sees you skipping breakfast.
best.art: A retirement party in a small glittering theater, a tall broad-shouldered woman in her sixties with steel-gray hair wearing a pink corsage on a church dress, laughing as a long line of former students from every decade hug her one by one, a tall drag queen in a magenta sequin gown applauding, balloons and a long buffet table, warm gold stage light, wide shot

good.title: Lunch Is Over
good.text: The cafeteria goes quiet and the mystery meat stays in the drains where it belongs. The lunch lady is just a tired woman you pass in the hall with a cart of trays. You never quite learn why any of it happened. But you say thank you at the steam table every single day now, just in case it matters.
good.art: A sunny high school cafeteria at lunchtime, a teenager holding a tray and smiling up at a tall woman in a hairnet and white apron behind the steam table, her face tired and still, students chattering at long tables behind them, bright daylight through tall windows, medium shot across the serving line

bittersweet.title: Seconds
bittersweet.text: You survive, and the kids from the walk-in mostly thaw out, though a couple of them shiver all winter. Then Ruthanne retires without a word one Friday in November. No party, no card. By the time you think to look up her name in the payroll files, she has moved to a sister's place in Vallejo, and the Friday Night Lady never calls KGLM again.
bittersweet.art: An empty school cafeteria serving line on a gray November afternoon, a single folded hairnet left on the clean steel steam table beside a ladle, chairs upturned on the tables, a teenager standing alone at the end of the line with a backpack, flat gray light through the tall windows, medium wide shot

bad.title: Tray, Fork, Napkin
bad.text: On November first you're behind the steam table in a hairnet and a stained apron, serving. Nobody looks up at you. Your crew comes through the line on Monday and takes their trays and doesn't recognize your face. You open your mouth to say your name, and all that comes out is the word next.
bad.art: A teenager in a hairnet and a stained apron stands behind a school cafeteria steam table holding a ladle with a blank face, and their three friends shuffle past in the lunch line with heads down staring at their trays, fluorescent light, long steel counter, medium shot from the students' side of the line
